why: Real B1 mistake (*is wanting*; the card's watch line: state verbs stay simple); the three right sentences are about three different things; the explanation uses this task's own sentence.

The instruction named the meaning and so gave the answer away, and without it *walked* is correct English. Dropped the instruction and replaced *walked* with *was walk*, a mistake the past_continuous card lists (*I [[was work]] when he called*).

fix.q: Choose the correct option: I ___ along the street when I saw an old friend.
fix.why: The walk was already going on when I saw my friend: *I was walking along the street when I saw an old friend.* The short action (*saw*) interrupts it.
fix.why_lv: Pastaiga jau notika, kad ieraudzīju draugu: *I was walking along the street when I saw an old friend.* Īsā darbība (*saw*) to pārtrauc.

why: Already a learning task, but *I will start waiting in an hour from now* is not a believable misunderstanding. Replaced it with a habit reading, which a learner could really pick.

wrong: I waited for an hour last week, then left.
I wait for an hour every day.
I waited an hour, but that was years ago.

why: *How long have they waited?* changes the given verb form; the task asks for a question about *They have been waiting*, so only that form is the answer.

*The project has finished.* is correct English (finish without an object) and close in meaning, so it cannot be a wrong option. Replaced it with *has being finished*, the card's watch line (*been*, not *being*).

fix.why: *has been* + 3rd form: *The project has been finished.* *Project* is singular, so *has*; and *been*, not *being*.
fix.why_lv: *has been* + 3. forma: *The project has been finished.* *Project* ir vienskaitlī, tāpēc *has*; un *been*, nevis *being*.

why: Gate long_frame and reader: the frame was needed only because *Someone checks the files on Monday* is correct English. Removed the frame and that option; the wrong options are now the card's mistakes (*will announced*, *will be tell*) plus a dropped passive.

fix.correct: The files will be checked on Monday.
wrong: The files will checked on Monday.
The files will be check on Monday.
fix.why: *will be* + 3rd form: *The files will be checked on Monday.* We do not say who checks them.
fix.why_lv: *will be* + 3. forma: *The files will be checked on Monday.* Mēs nesakām, kas tos pārbaudīs.

why: Correct, but far too easy for B1.2: only *Will* goes with *be explained*, and *Do / Are / Have* are rejected at once.
Learning task; *We booked early* and *We booked it early* were near-copies. Replaced the second with a believable misreading of the result clause (*We got a cheaper flight*).

Both natural orders are already accepted. Reader 2's orders (*the alarm goes off if everyone leaves the building*) turn cause and result around and make no sense here; reader 2's other answers were the key itself (list format).

The fronted *because* clause is natural and means the same (both clause orders around *because* are accepted). Rejected: *he said he was ill because he couldn't come* and *he couldn't come because he said he was ill* (other meaning), and reader 1's order with *he said* at the end (needs a comma, unnatural).
accept: because he was ill he said he couldn't come

why: The sentence stays: *next week → the next week* after a past reporting verb is correct reported speech (card: *tomorrow → the next day*), and placing *the* is the point. The explanation did not talk about this sentence at all; new explanation with its own sentence.

fix.why: After *told* the tense goes one step back and the time word changes: *'I'm leaving next week'* → *She told us that she was leaving the next week.*
fix.why_lv: Pēc *told* laiks iet vienu soli atpakaļ un mainās laika vārds: *'I'm leaving next week'* → *She told us that she was leaving the next week.*

why: Only *if I was* fits; the card teaches *asked* + *if / whether* + statement order. The wrong options are the card's mistakes (question order, *that*).
Both readers' fronted *every sunday* orders are natural English and mean the same; the two clause orders are already accepted.
accept: every sunday we used to visit my grandparents when i was a child
when i was a child every sunday we used to visit my grandparents

why: *Did ... used to* is the card's listed mistake (*I didn't [[used to]] like fish*), so *used* is a valid wrong card; *Do ... use* is wrong for a past habit.
*didn't used to* is the card's listed mistake (*I didn't [[used to]] like fish*); the teacher allows it as a wrong option (11 November).
Both clause orders are already accepted; reader 2's flag came from its list format.
Too easy for B1.1: *Who did* / *What did* before *phoned* are rejected at once. The explanation also used another sentence (*Who called?*); new explanation with this task's sentence.

fix.why: *Who* is the subject here (someone phoned you), so there is no *did*: *Who phoned you this morning?*
fix.why_lv: *Who* šeit ir teikuma priekšmets (kāds tev zvanīja), tāpēc *did* nav: *Who phoned you this morning?*

why: It tests the card's own point ("*can* has no future or perfect form: use *be able to*") and its listed mistake *will can*; fine for B1.1.

*by someone* is redundant but correct and must be accepted (as in the umbrella task); *could've* added. *prevented* changes the verb and is rejected. The explanation used other sentences; new one with this sentence.

answers: The accident could have been avoided.
The accident could have been avoided by someone.
The accident could've been avoided by someone.
fix.why: modal + *have been* + 3rd form: *The accident could have been avoided.* *by someone* is not needed.
fix.why_lv: Modālais darbības vārds + *have been* + 3. forma: *The accident could have been avoided.* *by someone* nav vajadzīgs.

why: *amaze / amazes* are verbs and can be rejected without knowing the point (*an* also helps). Rewritten so only *-ing / -ed* decides, both forms in one sentence, from the card's rule (*-ing* causes the feeling, *-ed* has it).

fix.correct: It was an amazing experience, and we were all amazed.
wrong: It was an amazed experience, and we were all amazing.
It was an amazing experience, and we were all amazing.
It was an amazed experience, and we were all amazed.
fix.why: *-ing* = what causes the feeling: *an amazing experience*. *-ed* = how people feel: *we were all amazed*.
fix.why_lv: *-ing* = kas izraisa sajūtu: *an amazing experience*. *-ed* = kā cilvēki jūtas: *we were all amazed*.

why: *in a beautiful old stone cottage they live* is not a natural order (fronted phrase, 4 November rule). Adjective order is on the B1.2 card.
Learning task; only one pairing works (*so many* + countable *people*, *so much* + *noise*, *such a* + noun phrase).
*would you like to drink something* is correct English with the same cards and meaning.
accept: would you like to drink something

why: *How often do the machines check?* has no object and makes no sense; only *are checked* fits.
Matching by world knowledge (what glass or paper is made from); the form is the same in all four (*is made*), so the form never decides (rule of 21 November). Needs a new task.
Both orders are already accepted; reader 2's flag came from its list format.
The contraction *My umbrella's been taken.* is correct and the checker does not work out *'s*. *stolen* changes the verb: rejected.
accept: My umbrella's been taken by someone.

why: Learning task; each passive matches only its own active sentence.

*In your language, what does this word mean?* is correct and natural. Rejected: *what does this word in your language mean* (unnatural) and *what does your word mean in this language* (other meaning).
accept: in your language what does this word mean

why: Only *employs* and *has* fit; *is having* is a real B1 mistake with a state verb.
Correct, but a basic fact in the present simple is an A2 point; too easy for B1.1.
*before he has made* does not fit a habit with *usually*; only *checks / makes*.
Correct, but a *How often* question in the present simple is an A2 point; too easy for B1.1.
Learning task (already practice); one pairing only, the verb decides the ending.
Learning task (already practice); each answer fits only one question.
Gate order: the statement is not possible here, but the readers' three other orders are natural and mean the same.
accept: can i take this chair or are you using it
are you using it or can i take this chair
can i take it or are you using this chair

why: *opens* (timetable) does not fit *so everything is chaotic this week*; *was opening* clashes with *is*. Only *is opening*.
*didn't finish yet* is American informal; with *yet* the task is about the present perfect, so only *hasn't finished*.
Swapping endings breaks the verb (*I have never tried so tired*), so only one pairing; learning task.
Learning task; *we had dinner* means dinner started after she arrived, so only *were having* matches 'already started'.
*So I stopped* is what makes the walk an action in progress; without it *walked* would fit. It is needed, and only *was walking* is accepted.
*The house was dirty* sets a past moment: *haven't cleaned* is wrong, and *didn't clean it for weeks* does not show the time before then. Only the past perfect.
All four orders are already accepted.
*when it was raining we left the house* is the other clause order of an accepted answer (*we left the house when it was raining*).
accept: when it was raining we left the house

why: Correct, but *yesterday* with three options makes *had to* obvious; too easy for B1.1.
*wasn't able to* is correct and means the same here.
Correct, but *was* for *be* at that moment is trivial for B1.2.
